concerns.text: FR-001 references “(See US-1)” but no identifier US-1 is defined anywhere; the user stories are labeled “User Story 1”. This cross‑reference is undefined.
FR-002 also cites “(See US-1)” – same undefined reference as above.
FR-003 cites “(See US-2)” but there is no US-2 identifier; the corresponding user story is “User Story 2”.
FR-004 cites “(See US-3)” yet no US-3 identifier exists; the related user story is “User Story 3”.
FR-006 mentions “(See US-2, US-3)” – both identifiers are undefined.
FR-007 again points to “(See US-1)” – undefined.

FR-002 states that missing values are handled by *filtering for complete cases*, while the Edge Cases section says missing metabolite‑class columns should be *imputed with zeros or excluded*. These two behaviours are mutually exclusive and create a functional contradiction.
Inconsistent terminology: the narrative uses “User Story 1/2/3” but the functional requirements refer to “US‑1/US‑2/US‑3”. This destabilizes traceability and may cause confusion.

SC-005 states a runtime limit (6‑hour) but does not describe how the runtime will be measured (e.g., wall‑clock time on the CI runner, logging method). Add a concrete measurement procedure to make the criterion verifiable.

The phrase “standard CPU” is vague; without a defined hardware baseline the 15‑minute completion target cannot be reliably measured. Specify the exact CPU model or benchmark environment to ensure the success criterion is measurable.

The idea explicitly expects the analysis to identify 3‑5 metabolite classes that show statistically significant *negative* correlation with herbivory (p < 0.05). The spec’s FR‑003 only requires computing a correlation matrix and producing a heatmap; it does not require extracting or reporting the subset of classes that meet the significance and direction criteria.

SC‑003 measures the false discovery rate of significant correlations but does not mandate reporting which metabolite classes are significant nor that they be negative. This leaves a gap between the idea’s expected result (list of 3‑5 biomarkers) and the spec’s success criteria.

The current design treats each plant species as an independent data point in correlation, regression, and Random Forest analyses, but does not account for phylogenetic non-independence. Ignoring shared evolutionary history can inflate type I error and bias effect size estimates. Incorporate a phylogenetically informed statistical approach (e.g., phylogenetic generalized least squares, mixed models with a species‑level random effect, or phylogenetic eigenvector regression) to ensure the validation targets (correlations, regression coefficients, R²) are independent of the predictor structure.

new_concerns.text: SC-001 states the number of plant species is measured against “the target of an appropriate sample size of species” – the target is undefined, making the criterion non‑measurable. Specify a concrete threshold (e.g., ≥ 50 species) or reference the FR‑001 minimum.

Correlation analysis (FR‑003) should incorporate a phylogenetically informed method (e.g., phylogenetic independent contrasts or phylogenetic generalized least‑squares correlation) to ensure that the identified significant negative correlations are not artefacts of shared ancestry.

The Random Forest regressor (FR‑005) does not include any mechanism to control for phylogenetic non‑independence. Consider either (a) using a phylogenetically structured cross‑validation scheme, (b) incorporating phylogenetic eigenvectors as additional predictors, or (c) explicitly stating the limitation and justifying why the model is still appropriate.
